summary: Describes use cases for a Path Computation Element acting as a central controller in a software-defined network. A PCE computes paths for traffic, and here it also supplies them to the devices that carry the traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: One traffic planner works out the best routes for a whole city and tells each junction what to do. This lists situations where that helps.

questions: use cases for pce as a central controller
subtitle: How a central controller can compute and install network traffic paths.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to steer traffic along optimal paths, but doing this with distributed protocols across many routers is complex. Controllers must decide paths while devices carry them out, creating a coordination problem.
tldr.mechanism: PCECC (PCE as a Central Controller) puts path computation and control in one place. A central PCE computes paths based on the network's full topology, then uses PCEP to download instructions to routers, which carry out the decisions.
tldr.outcome: Operators can simplify network management and optimization by centralizing path computation while keeping the network itself flexible. This works for many types of traffic engineering, from MPLS tunnels to segment routing to service chaining.

facts.label: Technology scope
facts.value: MPLS, SR, SRv6, Multicast, SFC, BIER, Native IP

today: RFC 9689 is an active Informational RFC. It catalogs use cases for PCECC; the actual protocol extensions are defined in companion RFCs (RFC 9050 for basic PCECC, RFC 8664 for SR, etc.). The RFC has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: PCE and the Move to Central Control
sections.content:
Networks grow more complex. To optimize traffic and avoid congestion, operators use Traffic Engineering (TE) to steer traffic away from shortest paths toward underused links. Traditionally, this required signalling protocols like RSVP-TE to negotiate paths hop-by-hop across the network. The Path Computation Element (PCE) separated path computation from the routers, letting a central engine calculate optimal paths. Now PCECC (PCE as a Central Controller) takes the next step: it computes paths and installs them directly.

PCECC shifts from distributed control to centralized instructions. Instead of routers cooperatively signalling each other, the PCE tells each router exactly what to do via PCEP (the PCE Communication Protocol). The PCE sees the full network topology and can compute disjoint backup paths, load-balance traffic, and manage the entire forwarding plane without signalling overhead. This is an element of Software-Defined Networking (SDN): a centralized system programs the forwarding behavior of network devices.

PCECC works with many technologies: MPLS label-switched paths, Segment Routing, service function chains, multicast, and native IP routing. This document catalogs the use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each traffic sign deciding independently where cars should go, one control center sees the whole network, picks the best route, and tells each sign what to display.

sections.title: MPLS Label Management and Segment Routing
sections.content:
MPLS uses labels (short numeric tags) to forward packets. Traditional MPLS labels are either assigned locally at each router using protocols like LDP, or negotiated across a path using RSVP-TE. PCECC simplifies this: the central controller assigns labels and distributes them.

For traditional MPLS tunnels, the PCECC controls label space on the routers it manages. When it computes a tunnel, it tells each router along the path what labels to use on each link, what traffic to accept, and how to forward. This is called static TE LSP (Label-Switched Path) provisioning.

For Segment Routing (SR), the PCECC allocates Segment Identifiers (SIDs)—globally meaningful labels or IPv6 addresses—and distributes them to routers. Once routers have SIDs, the PCE can send an ingress router a list of SIDs (the segment path) to push onto traffic. Intermediate routers follow the SID list based on pre-learned routing, removing labels (pop) as they process each segment. This works for both SR-MPLS (using MPLS labels as SIDs) and SRv6 (using IPv6 addresses as SIDs).

SR with PCECC enables SR Policies: the PCE computes multiple candidate paths and provisions them as policies the ingress router can select based on traffic requirements. The PCE can also allocate Binding SIDs (BSIDs) for efficient traffic steering into policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of routers locally deciding which numbers to use for labels, the PCE issues numbers and distributes them. For Segment Routing, the PCE gives each router its segment numbers and can tell the ingress what sequence to use.

sections.title: Load Balancing, Protection, and Multi-Domain Paths
sections.content:
PCECC excels when complex coordination is needed across many nodes or domains.

Load Balancing: Service providers often need multiple parallel tunnels from one point to another with load-sharing across them. The PCECC can compute N disjoint (non-overlapping) paths according to constraints—avoiding specific links, meeting bandwidth requirements, or satisfying other objectives. It provisions all N tunnels to the ingress router, which then balances traffic across them. The PCE continuously monitors network state and can recompute paths when bandwidth demand changes.

Protection (Fast Reroute): When a link or node fails, traffic should switch to a backup path in milliseconds. With PCECC, primary paths are computed along with disjoint backup paths, and both are pre-installed at the ingress. When failure detection occurs, the router switches to the backup without waiting for the network to converge. The PCE can also set up local protection at every intermediate router: when a router detects the next hop has failed, it immediately swaps traffic to a locally precomputed bypass around that node.

Inter-AS Paths: When paths cross multiple autonomous systems (AS), PCECC bridges domains. The PCE maintains BGP-LS (Border Gateway Protocol - Link State) sessions with route reflectors in each domain to learn topology. It computes multi-domain paths respecting AS sequence constraints and preferred border routers, then programs the entry/exit ASBRs (AS Border Routers) to carry the traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE can calculate multiple safe routes and install them all. If the main route fails, traffic auto-switches to backup. For multi-country routes, the PCE understands each country's borders and rules.

sections.title: Multicast, Service Chaining, and Emerging Use Cases
sections.content:
PCECC's centralized view is especially valuable for complex packet handling.

Multicast (P2MP/MP2MP): Point-to-multipoint trees let one source send to many receivers. Computing and protecting these trees manually is error-prone. The PCECC computes primary and backup multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) trees, assigning labels at each branch point to replicate traffic. It also computes local protection bypasses around each node in the tree. All instructions are pre-installed; when a node fails, the Point of Local Repair immediately re-routes around it.

Service Function Chaining (SFC): Packets often need to pass through service functions (firewalls, load balancers, proxies) in a specific order. The PCE can compute service paths, classify traffic to identify which service chain applies, install the classification rules at entry points, and provision the forwarding path through all functions. PCEP extensions tell each service node which packets to process and what the next hop is.

Native IP Traffic Engineering: PCECC can work with plain BGP routing. The PCE instructs routers to set up multiple BGP sessions and distributes specific IP prefixes to different sessions. By controlling which next-hop each prefix uses, the PCE steers traffic without MPLS labels.

BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication): An emerging multicast scheme where receivers are encoded as a bitmap in the packet. PCECC allocates bit positions and programs routers with the tree topology implied by each bit, enabling efficient multicast without per-tree signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE can route traffic through service functions in the right order, send multicast trees to many places at once, or steer traffic by controlling which BGP routes look best.

sections.title: How PCECC Works
sections.content:
PCECC uses PCEP (PCE Communication Protocol) as the control protocol between the PCE and PCCs (Path Computation Clients—the routers). A router enabled for central control becomes a PCC, maintaining a persistent PCEP session with the PCE.

Topology Learning: The PCE learns the network topology from BGP-LS (Border Gateway Protocol - Link State), which routers use to flood link state information. The PCE consumes these advertisements and builds a full graph of the network, including link capacities, affinities, and other attributes.

Path Computation: When an application or operator requests a path (or when the PCE precomputes based on policy), the PCE runs a path algorithm subject to constraints: bandwidth, link/node affinities, latency, disjointness from other paths, and more. The PCE can optimize for various objectives (shortest path, least utilized links, best latency).

Installation: The PCE sends PCEP messages to the relevant routers. For PCECC-style LSPs, it sends PCInitiate messages to each router along the path with explicit label forwarding instructions. For Segment Routing, it sends SID lists. For load-balanced tunnels, it installs all paths to the ingress and the ingress performs the load-sharing.

Monitoring and Reoptimization: Routers report LSP status and actual link utilization back to the PCE via PCEP. The PCE continuously checks for congestion or failures and computes new paths to reoptimize.

Security: PCEP sessions should use TLS for encryption and authentication, ensuring the PCE's instructions cannot be intercepted or forged. Policies can restrict what each PCE can control.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers tell the PCE what the network looks like. The PCE picks the best path, then sends instructions to each router. Routers report back if there are problems.

sections.title: Benefits and Design Considerations
sections.content:
Benefits of PCECC:

  • Simplified operations: No need to manually configure paths or manage distributed signalling. The PCE handles coordination.
  • Optimal paths: The PCE sees the full network state and can compute globally optimal paths in real time.
  • Reduced complexity: No complex signalling protocols like RSVP-TE; routers simply execute instructions.
  • Fast protection: Pre-installed backup paths enable sub-second reroute on failure.
  • Flexibility: PCECC works with many technologies (MPLS, SR, IPv6, multicast) and can be deployed incrementally.

Design Considerations:

  • Central point of failure: The PCE itself must be robust. Deployments typically use multiple PCEs with redundancy and failover.
  • Convergence time: If the PCE is slow to react to failures, traffic may be delayed. BGP-LS advertisements and PCE computation must be fast.
  • Scalability: A single PCE has limits on the number of routers and paths it can manage. Large networks may use hierarchical or distributed PCE architectures.
  • Incremental deployment: PCECC works alongside legacy routers. During network migration, some routers use distributed protocols while others are PCE-controlled.

The RFC emphasizes that PCECC is a framework: specific PCEP extensions are defined in companion documents for each technology (SR, BIER, SFC, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: PCECC makes network control simpler and faster, but the PCE must be reliable and responsive. It can coexist with old-style routers during migration.
